fatal_errors: The proposed vanadium addition does not reconstruct the target intervention, which varied Mo content in a Ni/MoS2-Ag-Cr2O3 self-lubricating CoCrFeNiMox composite.
Evidence E1 concerns Al0.7CoCrFeNiV0.5, not CoCrFeNi with 0.5 atomic percent V; V0.5 denotes a much larger nominal compositional fraction than 0.5 at.%.
Neither cited source supports stable vanadium-derived lubrication or simultaneous friction and wear reduction from room temperature through 800 °C.
The assertion that 0.5 at.% V will convert CoCrFeNi into a homogeneous BCC-dominated alloy is unsupported and scientifically implausible from the cited evidence.
The proposed mechanism omits the distinct low-temperature MoS2/Ag lubrication and high-temperature oxide/silver-molybdate glaze responsible for the target wide-temperature behavior.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the broad engineering objective and proposes a nominally testable alloying intervention, but it is not a reconstruction of the reported material system. The target relies on increasing Mo in a multicomponent self-lubricating composite, producing FCC lattice distortion and a hard Mo-rich sigma phase, with MoS2/Ag films at lower temperatures and compact NiO/silver-molybdate glazes at high temperatures. The generated hypothesis instead extrapolates vanadium results from an Al-containing HEA to nearly V-free CoCrFeNi and assumes BCC homogenization and lubricious oxidation without direct support. Its baseline description is also weak because CoCrFeNi is generally FCC-dominated rather than intrinsically dual-phase. Conditions are insufficiently specified: there is no exact load, speed, counterface, distance, or discrete temperature schedule. The baseline-versus-V experiment, XRD/SEM/XPS characterization, and explicit falsification rule provide some discriminability, but a continuous temperature ramp introduces thermal-history confounding and the design lacks replication and fixed tribological parameters. Overall, this is an inadequately supported alternative rather than a plausible evidence-based solution to the full-temperature problem.
